title: DDP with DataLoader num_workers>0 seems to result in GIL (CPU summing to 100%)
body:
### Bug description

When running the pl Trainer with ddp on a single node with multiple gpus and DataLoader(..., num_workers=2) (or >0) CPU use seems to max at 100% - when num_woerkers=0 it will go much higher.

Running the below boring model results in very slow data loading with htop outputs like this:
![image](https://github.com/Lightning-AI/lightning/assets/46681532/418742c8-8c06-40f5-a0e4-fe1e53af3c12)


It looks like there are 100%/16 workes = ~6.25% each

On the other hand if I run it with num_workers=0 I get faster training and much better CPU utilisation:
![image](https://github.com/Lightning-AI/lightning/assets/46681532/56577d2a-8a24-49d1-bfbe-daa2583ce758)



When using num_workers=0 in practice with more complex dataloading workflows it is still a bottleneck (but still better utilisation than n>0).

Additionally the docs seem to suggest setting num_workers=num_cpus however it seems like num_workers is per device?

Any help/advice would be appreciated!

### What version are you seeing the problem on?

v2.0

### How to reproduce the bug

```python
import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.nn import functional as F
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, Dataset
import pytorch_lightning as pl
tmpdir = os.getcwd()


class RandomDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, shape, num_samples) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.shape = shape
        self.num_samples = num_samples
    
    def __len__(self):
        return self.num_samples
    
    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        return torch.randn(self.shape)**(5/4)

num_samples = 10000
train = RandomDataset((3, 2048, 2048), num_samples)
train = DataLoader(train, batch_size=32, pin_memory=True, num_workers=2)
val = RandomDataset((3, 2048, 2048), num_samples)
val = DataLoader(val, batch_size=32, pin_memory=True, num_workers=2)

class BoringModel(pl.LightningModule):

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.layer = torch.nn.Conv2d(3, 1, 1)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.layer(x)

    def loss(self, batch, prediction):
        return torch.nn.functional.mse_loss(prediction, torch.ones_like(prediction))

    def training_step(self, batch, batch_idx):
        output = self.layer(batch)
        loss = self.loss(batch, output)
        self.log('train_loss', loss)
        return loss


    def validation_step(self, batch, batch_idx):
        output = self.layer(batch)
        loss = self.loss(batch, output)
        return {"x": loss}


    def test_step(self, batch, batch_idx):
        output = self.layer(batch)
        loss = self.loss(batch, output)
        self.log('test_loss', loss)
        return {"y": loss}


    def configure_optimizers(self):
        optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(self.layer.parameters(), lr=0.1)
        lr_scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.StepLR(optimizer, step_size=1)
        return [optimizer], [lr_scheduler]

def test(tmpdir):
    # init model
    model = BoringModel()

    # Initialize a trainer
    trainer = pl.Trainer(
        accelerator='gpu',
        strategy='ddp',
        devices=8,
        max_epochs=1,
        precision='bf16-mixed',
        default_root_dir=tmpdir
    )

    trainer.fit(model, train)

test(tmpdir)
```

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: @reporter With a simple data preprocessing like you show `return torch.randn(self.shape)**(5/4)`, the process communication will dominate and is likely the reason why you see better performance with `num_workers=0`. To be sure, we could convert the example you gave to regular PyTorch code to show the same behavior (I would expect it to show the same results).

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
@reporter Could you take a look at this raw PyTorch example:

```py
import os

import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, Dataset


class RandomDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, shape, num_samples) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.shape = shape
        self.num_samples = num_samples

    def __len__(self):
        return self.num_samples

    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        arr = torch.randn(self.shape) ** (5 / 4)
        # for x in torch.randn(30000):
        #     arr *= x
        return arr


class BoringModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.layer = torch.nn.Conv2d(3, 1, 1)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.layer(x)


def run(rank, world_size):
    cuda = True  # change here
    torch.manual_seed(1)
    device = torch.device("cuda", rank) if cuda else torch.device("cpu")
    if cuda:
        torch.cuda.manual_seed(1)
        torch.cuda.set_device(device)

    os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"] = str(rank)
    os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"] = str(world_size)
    os.environ["MASTER_ADDR"] = "localhost"
    os.environ["MASTER_PORT"] = "1234"
    torch.distributed.init_process_group(
        backend=("nccl" if cuda else "gloo"),
        init_method="env://",
        rank=rank,
        world_size=world_size,
    )
    print("init rank done", rank)

    train = RandomDataset((3, 2048, 2048), 10000)
    train = DataLoader(
        train, 
        batch_size=32, 
        pin_memory=True, 
        num_workers=0,  # change here
    )

    model = BoringModel().to(device)
    ddp_model = DistributedDataParallel(model, device_ids=([rank] if cuda else None))
    optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(ddp_model.parameters(), lr=0.1)

    print("start training")
    for i, batch in enumerate(train):
        print(i)
        batch = batch.to(device)
        prediction = ddp_model(batch)
        loss = torch.nn.functional.mse_loss(prediction, torch.ones_like(prediction))
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    world_size = 4  # change here
    torch.multiprocessing.spawn(run, nprocs=world_size, args=(world_size, ))

```

Set the `world_size`, `num_workers` and `cuda` flags as you like. This demonstrates the same behavior as described with the PL model. We are running on different systems, so if you could verify the observations:

- num_workers=2 => peak per-process usage is 100%, but GPU can overlap with data loading
- num_workers=0 => torch uses multiple cores in the main process directly (>100% usage), but CPU blocking the GPU

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
Hey @reporter 
Sorry I left you hanging. 

> Am I right in thinking that this script is ~equivalent to running with ddp_spwan in pl? 

Yes!

> That runs fine with num_workers>0 it's the pure ddp that doesn't and is apparently faster/better (than ddp_spawn) according to the docs?

Sure, here is what we need to do to the script I posted to simulate the "pure DDP" that Lightning does. Change the bottom part of the script with this:


```py
if __name__ == "__main__":
    rank = int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"])
    run(rank, world_size=4)
```
Then invoke several processes in parallel like so:
    
```bash
LOCAL_RANK=0  python examples/dataloader_bench.py & LOCAL_RANK=1  python examples/datal
oader_bench.py & LOCAL_RANK=2  python examples/dataloader_bench.py & LOCAL_RANK=3  python examples/dataloader_bench.py
```
(replacing the script name)

And on my system this shows the same behavior:
- num_workers=0 -> All dataloading is done in main process, torch is distributing its computation over several cores -> CPU shows usage 4000% or similar in htop
- num_workers>0 -> Each dataloader worker runs in its own process, there will be a total of `num_workers * num gpus` in total, and each will max out at around 100% as seen in htop

To the best of my abilities, I cannot determine any inconsistencies when running the raw PyTorch script and comparing it to the PL version. 


> Also while you're here - the docs suggest that you should use num_workers=num_cpus but in practice it seems to be num_workers per device/process (that script gave up to ~2400%CPU = 8 main + 28dl? Def more than 8 + 2 dl workers) - you presumably don't want 308 = 240 dl workers on a 30 core, 8 card machine?

Yes, num_workers should be chosen per GPU. Example: 1 dataloader with num_workers=4, devices=8, num_nodes=2 -> there will be a total of 4*8= 32 dataloading processes. The docs suggestion is maybe a bit controversial, I agree.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: I think I found it by the way! For some reason if, as in the scripts above, I don't explicitly set the Dataloader multiprocessing_context it defaults to None even with num_workers >0. If I set it to any of the options eg 'forkserver' or 'spawn' it works properly. I'm not sure why the default doesn't work but might be worth a bug fix or at least documentation change?

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: It is normal for `DataLoader.multiprocessing_context` to be None by default if you didn't explicitly set it. None there simply means that Pytorch will use the default depending on the operating system, and on Linux it will be "fork". I don't know why switching to a different one explicitly would make such a drastic difference for you.

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
I have been digging into this issue for days and @reporter's solution also worked for me!

**TL;DR** If you are seeing the dataloader processes in low CPU utils, much slower than setting ``num_workers=0`` and loading data in the main thread, set ``multiprocessing_context='spawn'`` when you are creating the DataLoader.

The reason why it matters might be found in [this blog post](https://pythonspeed.com/articles/faster-multiprocessing-pickle/). As it suggests,
> the "fork" context is super-broken, which is why it will stop being the default in Python 3.14.
>
> On my computer, this program (with "fork") consistently deadlocks: it freezes and never exits. Any time you have threads in the parent process, the "fork" context can cause in potential deadlocks, or even corrupted memory, in the child process.

So IMO ``"spawn"`` should be preferred in practice and please try this if you are facing similar issues!

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: It's definitely interesting that you were able to get into this case where `multiprocessing_context` has such a dramatic effect. I suggest we close the ticket, since Lightning probably can't do much here as the default for this is platform specific and set by PyTorch. If you believe this could affect a considerable amount of users, we could try to get some advice from the PyTorch team.
